newsitem.title: USA: NASA plans to patch up tattered Hubble telescope.
newsitem.headline: NASA plans to patch up tattered Hubble telescope.

text.p: NASA flight controllers on Sunday recommended an extra spacewalk from shuttle Discovery to patch up the Hubble Space Telescope's torn and tattered exterior.

Scientists were concerned the ripped silvery foil, which offered protection against the harsh environment of space, could peel off, causing crucial electronics to overheat and rendering the telescope inoperable.

Flight director Jeff Bantle told the astronauts they would make their fourth spacewalk on Sunday night to finish their preplanned servicing tasks and then start repairs on two long rips in the foil near the top of the telescope. An extra spacewalk on Monday night would be made to place patches over three compartments containing electronics.
"That makes a lot of sense to us," shuttle commander Ken Bowersox said. "We like what you've got for a plan now."

Engineers and astronauts on the ground were devising ways to tie patches over four areas of the telescope's exterior. The repair kit would be improvised from spare foil, adhesive tape, ropes, electrical wire and clips.
Jerry Ross, a veteran of four spacewalks, was to test the procedure first on a mock-up of the telescope in a water tank near the Johnson Space Centre.
Earlier, Mark Lee and Steve Smith, making the third spacewalk of the mission, took a closeup look at some of the damage.

"Basically this thing is just falling apart, cracking all over the place," Lee told mission control as he inspected a foil-covered door on the telescope. He tried taping up a crack but as NASA engineers had feared the adhesive failed to hold.
"It barely sticks," he said. "It doesn't do anything."
Lee and Smith collected pieces of spare foil, tape and cords aboard the shuttle for the possible repair attempt.

Engineers suspected variations in temperature and ultraviolet rays from the sun had caused the silvery foil to crack and tear. The damage, which appeared extensive, was not seen when astronauts last visited the telescope in 1993.

Lee and Smith upgraded three more components of the telescope during their seven-hour spacewalk. They completed what was considered the most challenging task of the effort, the replacement of a faulty electronics box.

The swap-out of the data interface unit, which relays computer commands to various telescope components, was difficult because the device was not designed to be handled by astronauts wearing bulky space suit gloves.
Working in a jumble of wires, Lee had to make 18 cable connections to complete the installation. "Great hands, Mark," mission control's Jeff Hoffman radioed once the work was done.
The two men then went on to exchange an ageing reel-to-reel tape recorder for a new digital model and replace a broken flywheel used to manoeuvre the telescope.
"You guys are batting 100 percent," mission control's Marc Garneau radioed as the two men completed their work.
Between tasks, the astronauts marvelled at the spectacular view as the shuttle soared more than 370 miles (595 km) above the Pacific, off the west coast of Australia.
"Holy cow!" Lee exclaimed. "I've got the Hubble Space Telescope, Shark's Bay, and the planet Earth and the moon in my view. What a great place to be."
"Just an average day for a couple of spacewalkers," Joe Tanner remarked from inside the shuttle's cabin.

As the astronauts ended their spacewalk, shuttle commander Ken Bowersox and copilot Scott Horowitz fired the smallest manoeuvring jets aboard for 20 minutes to nudge Hubble into a higher orbit. NASA hopes to boost the telescope's altitude by a total of five miles (8 km) to prolong its lifetime.
